caseStudies.title: Removing DTC from a distributed orchestrator
caseStudies.summary: Re-architected a Temporal.io orchestrator to drop its distributed transaction coordinator dependency, unblocking a service estate frozen on legacy .NET runtimes and cutting the upgrade cycle from 5-7 days to 3.
caseStudies.problem: The platform's orchestration layer depended on a distributed transaction coordinator to keep multi-service operations consistent. That dependency pinned services to old runtimes — .NET Core 2.2 and .NET Framework 4.5 — because the coordinator's behaviour could not be carried forward cleanly. Every attempted upgrade risked correctness, so the estate stayed frozen and the cost of change kept rising. Understanding and upgrading a single system cycle took 5 to 7 working days.
caseStudies.approach: I led the re-architecture of the platform's Temporal.io orchestrator so that consistency no longer relied on a distributed transaction coordinator, replacing ambient transactional guarantees with explicit orchestration on its durable-execution model. Rather than treat each service as a one-off, I authored a transformation project template and the rules governing it, so every later module started from a known-good shape instead of a blank page. I then built a set of AI skills and a workflow over them that guided engineers through the transformation — encoding the decisions that were otherwise re-derived by hand on every module. I led the rollout inside my own team and ran sessions with other teams migrating the same way.
outcomes: A single upgrade cycle fell from 5-7 working days to a maximum of 3.
5 modules modernized, with a repeatable template for the rest.
Company award for the resulting time and cost saving.
Other teams adopted the same template and workflow.

caseStudies.title: Making AI usable by engineers and non-engineers alike
caseStudies.shortTitle: Making AI usable across a company
caseStudies.summary: Took AI from ad-hoc use to production: trained non-technical departments (SME recognition), shipped an autonomous Copilot Studio agent, and built the AI-guided workflow that cut upgrade cycles from 5-7 days to 3.
caseStudies.problem: AI tooling was available but unevenly used. Engineers applied it ad hoc with inconsistent results, and non-technical departments such as HR had no route into it at all — the tools assumed a technical vocabulary their work never required.
caseStudies.approach: I treated this as two different problems rather than one. For non-technical staff I designed and delivered a course pitched at their actual workflows instead of at the tooling, which is what earned the subject matter expert recognition. For engineering I went further than training: I built AI skills and an orchestrating workflow that encoded the modernization decisions directly, so the guidance lived in the process rather than in someone's memory. Alongside this I shipped an autonomous agent on Microsoft Copilot Studio, now in production use.
outcomes: Subject matter expert recognition for the AI training course.
Autonomous agent on Microsoft Copilot Studio, in production use.
AI-guided modernization workflow that cut the upgrade cycle from 5-7 days to a maximum of 3.
Development team mentored on applying AI tooling to daily engineering work.

caseStudies.title: Windoor Wizard Builder — a fabrication engine that has to be exactly right
caseStudies.summary: A multi-tenant SaaS for Egyptian UPVC window and door workshops, merging a commercial quoting and production platform with a cutting-optimisation engine verified against a real shop floor.
caseStudies.problem: Egyptian UPVC workshops run on WhatsApp, Excel, and paper. Quotes are priced by hand, cut lists are worked out per job, and the profile offcuts that decide whether a job is profitable are estimated rather than calculated. Generic ERP does not help because it does not model the domain — it has no concept of a frame deduction registry, bar nesting, or the glass area and steel reinforcement that drive real cost. A workshop running generic software still does the hard part on paper.
caseStudies.approach: Three decisions carry this system. First, lengths are stored as exact integer tenths of a millimetre rather than as decimals: the shop cuts half-millimetres — 44 of 195 verified rows — and a rounded cut list produces a window that does not fit. The value type deliberately exposes no decimal factory, so rounding cannot enter the model at all; the wrong thing is unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged. Second, bar nesting is one-dimensional bin packing, so it uses First-Fit-Decreasing, with the three details that separate a real implementation from the textbook one: saw kerf charged per cut, loud failure on a piece longer than a bar rather than a best-effort list that cannot be executed, and a stable sort so two runs over one order produce identical cut lists. Every constant — bar length, end trim, kerf, minimum reusable offcut — is supplied by the caller, so a different workshop is configuration rather than code. Third, the engine became a bounded context inside the SaaS rather than a service beside it, because its calculations always run inside a tenant's quote and share that transaction; a network boundary would have bought overhead and returned nothing. Tenant isolation is enforced by EF Core global query filters, not by a WHERE clause every query is trusted to remember.
outcomes: Two half-built systems merged into one .NET 10 monorepo: the SaaS had a stubbed pricing engine, the engine had no tenancy or persistence.
491 unit tests passing across domain, application, API, and infrastructure.
Cutting engine oracle-verified against real orders from a working workshop, not against assumptions derived from the same understanding that wrote the code.
72 pre-existing pricing failures kept and documented as the integration specification rather than deleted to make the suite green.
Arabic right-to-left throughout, in the interface and in generated PDFs.

caseStudies.title: Payment middleware across 9 countries
caseStudies.summary: A middleware reverse proxy unifying payment gateway integration across 9 countries, built on Clean Architecture with Strategy and Pipeline patterns.
caseStudies.problem: Payment integration had to work across nine countries, each with its own providers, rules, and failure modes. Integrating each market directly into the products would have multiplied the same logic nine times over and made every provider change a cross-cutting edit.
caseStudies.approach: I architected a middleware reverse proxy that gave the products one payment interface regardless of market. Provider-specific behaviour sits behind the Strategy pattern, so adding a country means adding a strategy rather than editing shared code. Cross-cutting concerns — validation, logging, error translation — run through a Pipeline. The whole thing follows Clean Architecture with CQRS, keeping the payment domain independent of both transport and provider SDKs.
outcomes: One integration surface serving 9 countries.
New providers onboarded by adding a strategy, without touching shared logic.
Cross-cutting concerns handled once in the pipeline rather than per provider.

caseStudies.title: Rebuilding a legacy MVC application as a .NET Web API
caseStudies.shortTitle: Rebuilding legacy MVC as a Web API
caseStudies.summary: A full rebuild of an ageing MVC application into a modern Web API, including a data access migration from Entity Framework to Dapper and a move onto Azure.
caseStudies.problem: An existing MVC application had accumulated enough structural debt that routine changes were slow and risky. Its data access layer and database schema had grown organically rather than by design, and query performance had become a recurring complaint.
caseStudies.approach: Rather than patch around it, I led a rebuild into a .NET Web API with a redesigned database structure. I replaced Entity Framework with Dapper in the hot paths, trading ORM convenience for explicit control over the SQL where performance mattered. I then supported the migration onto Azure, moving data processing and storage onto managed services.
outcomes: Legacy MVC application replaced by a maintainable Web API.
Query performance improved by moving hot paths from Entity Framework to Dapper.
Database structure redesigned to match how the system is actually used.
Application migrated onto Azure managed services.
